scenes.heading: Linear graphs from rules
scenes.sub: One rule, a whole straight line
scenes.say: How can one short rule draw a whole line? Today you'll turn rules like y equals two x plus one into tables, points and straight-line graphs.
scenes.caption: How can one short rule draw a whole line? Today you'll turn rules like y = 2x + 1 into tables, points and straight-line graphs.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Vending machine: press a button, get one snack
scenes.science: Rule y = 2x + 1: put in x, get exactly one y
scenes.breaks: A machine has a few buttons, but a rule takes any number, so the points fill an unbroken line.
scenes.say: A vending machine follows a rule. Press a button and you always get the same snack. A rule like y equals two x plus one is a number machine. Put in any x and out comes exactly one y. Each input and output make a point.
scenes.caption: A vending machine follows a rule. Press a button and you always get the same snack. A rule like y = 2x + 1 is a number machine. Put in any x and out comes exactly one y. Each input and output make a point.

scenes.heading: Graphing a rule
steps: Substitute each x to find y
Rule a straight line through them
scenes.say: To graph a rule, choose some x-values, including negatives and zero. Substitute each one to find y, putting brackets around negatives. Plot the points, then rule a straight line through them. Two points make the line, and a third checks it.

scenes.heading: Plot the table, rule the line
notes: Rule a line through them all
scenes.say: Here is y equals two x plus one. First the grid, then each point from the table: negative two, negative three, up to two, five. A ruler passes through every point, and the line crosses the y-axis at one, just as x equals zero said.
scenes.caption: y = 2x + 1: the points (−2, −3) to (2, 5) all sit on one straight line, crossing the y-axis at 1.

scenes.heading: Table for y = 4 − 2x
scenes.question: Find y for x = −1, 0, 1, 2 using y = 4 − 2x.
scenes.say: Use y equals four minus two x. When x is negative one, four minus two times negative one is four plus two, which is six. When x is zero, y is four. Then two, then zero. The y-values go down by two each time, so the line slopes downwards.
scenes.caption: Use y = 4 − 2x. When x = −1: 4 − 2 × (−1) = 4 + 2 = 6. When x = 0, y = 4. Then 2, then 0. y goes down by 2 each time, so the line slopes down.

scenes.heading: Where it crosses the axes
scenes.say: To find where a line crosses an axis, make the other letter zero. For the y-intercept, put x equals zero. For y equals two x minus six, that gives negative six. For the x-intercept, put y equals zero and solve: x equals three.
scenes.caption: To find where a line crosses an axis, make the other letter zero. For the y-intercept, put x = 0: y = 2x − 6 gives −6. For the x-intercept, put y = 0 and solve: x = 3.

scenes.heading: Flat or tall?
scenes.say: Some rules have only one letter. y equals two means every point has height two, so the line is flat. x equals negative three means every point is three to the left, so the line stands tall.
scenes.caption: Some rules have only one letter. y = 2 means every point has height 2, so the line is flat. x = −3 means every point is 3 to the left, so the line stands tall.

scenes.heading: y = 2 and x = −3
scenes.say: Watch the two special lines. y equals two is drawn flat, because y stays at two for every x. x equals negative three is drawn straight up and down, through negative three on the x-axis.
scenes.caption: y = 2 is horizontal through (0, 2). x = −3 is vertical through (−3, 0).

points: Substitute x to get y, then plot
On the line? Substitute and compare
Intercepts: make the other letter zero
scenes.say: Quick recap. Substitute x to get y, then plot and rule a line. Put brackets around negatives. To test a point, substitute and compare. For intercepts, make the other letter zero. Now try the practice questions!
